endorsements.quote: Changes in indication of use, the level of autonomy of the system or performance drift, which might increase the level of risk, will require detailed evaluation.
Performance should be evaluated at regular intervals, with more frequent evaluations of rapidly changing systems.

Building on the IDEAL-D preclinical device assessment approach of relative risk assessment, the proportionate evaluation of autono mous surgical robots should be guided by its classification along two main axes—autonomy level and risk—before proceeding to clinical studies16,24.

Randomized controlled trials will serve as the default choice for thorough comparative studies of robotic surgery where preliminary studies suggest a potentially important clinical or economic benefit.

Robot assessment should include a human factors-based evaluation of team communication (including communication with the robot), intuitiveness of visual displays, control interface usability, feedback mechanisms (for example, haptic and auditory) and ease of integration with existing workflows.
In principle, a standard process for determining responsibility for errors when AI is integrated should be adopted with suitable expert advice and should be publicly accessible.
In systems with AI integration, the AI component is particularly susceptible to rapid iterations, and therefore changes to input data, algorithm code and model testing should be reported.
Conflicts of interest should be openly addressed35.
Sustainability metrics should be recorded during preclinical (device-only) and clinical (device within system) evaluations48.
Data should be collected and analyzed by groups independent from those producing it.
Reporting of technical failures (including software failures) and patient safety incidents should be mandatory, supported by national regulators and independent of device manufacturers.
A human factors expert should be included in the analysis of all serious adverse events involving a surgical robot.
Thresholds for this kind of action should be established in advance, considering trends in outcome data suggesting changes in risk levels, indications for use or device performance.

Active patient and public involvement is desirable to ensure a patient-centered research design from the outset, and formal qualitative research assessing patient perceptions, understanding of the robotic system and trust in the intervention may be very informative.
This should include monitoring for frequency of, and reasons for, surgical team members taking over control of the robotic system, alongside inde pendent observation and qualitative assessment.

Independent ethical advice should be sought to determine whether control groups for a randomized trial are acceptable, depending on the nature of the presumed benefits and anticipated risks of the procedure and the outcome data available.

Later stages (stage 1 and beyond) should study the performance of the AI algorithms within systems (with the hardware components of that system version) in a clinical context—using clinical outcomes where feasible.
Reporting guidelines, such as DECIDE-AI, should be used to guide early clinical evaluation30.

unlisted_practices: Evaluate AI-integrated surgical robots by first testing the autonomous component and hardware separately, then in silico and simulator-based assessment of the integrated system, before clinical study.
Disclose to patients in consent the level of AI autonomy, takeover protocols, system failure mitigation, surgical team experience, and conflicts of interest.
Evaluate the reliability of handover mechanisms and reasons for human takeover in autonomous systems.
Perform early and iterative health economic modeling and cost-effectiveness analysis of AI-enabled devices.
Conduct life cycle and sustainability assessments of AI-enabled surgical robots and compare against current standard treatment.
Preregister study protocols publicly and record post hoc changes.
Use an independent expert panel working with regulators to decide return to earlier evaluation stages after major risk changes.
Require regular revalidation and credentialing of surgeons using robotic systems, with training programs overseen by accrediting bodies independent of industry.

Establish clinical governance that allocates responsibility for monitoring, accountability for adverse events, and improvements for autonomous AI systems via collaboration among legislators, healthcare organizations, professional bodies, and industry.
Build international data-sharing surveillance registries with harmonized coding and FAIR-accessible analyses for long-term device monitoring.
Make registry and real-world evidence accessible to patients in lay language and inform consent with indication-specific evidence.
Learning curves should be evaluated and accounted for in comparative studies of robotic systems.
Record and describe iterative changes to device, procedure, and patient selection in a log accessible to regulators.
